content.text:
**No.** With this project and these tools, I can't give you real 3D swimming that stays faithful to your approved pictures from start to end with no visible differences. Here are the straight answers.

**1. Can I achieve both?** No. Your approved screen is one painting seen from one spot. Real 3D swimming needs a whole tunnel that can be seen from every position along the way. Everything your painting doesn't show (the sides, what's ahead, what's behind) has to be built or generated, and that part never matches the painting exactly. Every attempt in this project shows the same thing. The still painted screen measured about 94% like your picture. Every version where the camera really moves through 3D measured about 5–12%.

**2. Is there a technical solution different from what failed?** There is one thing not yet tried properly, and I can't promise it works. It uses World Labs Atlas, which is already connected. Atlas would generate many views travelling down your tunnel from your picture, then combine them into a photographic-style 3D scene. Benny would swim through it with a real follow-camera, with real flowing water and coins added on top. In November the project tried a simpler version, a 3D world made from your single picture. The far third of the tunnel and the S-curved river collapsed, so it wasn't usable. The multi-view method is the step up from that. Otherwise the industry answer is a dedicated 3D environment artist who builds the tunnel by hand in Blender from your painting.

**3. What differences would remain, even if it works?**
- Details further down the tunnel would be invented, not yours.
- Close-up areas could look soft or blurry.
- The glow and lighting would be flatter than the painting.
- The water would be animated, not your exact painted streaks.
- The S-curves may not follow your painting exactly.
- It might have to be simplified to run smoothly on cheaper Android phones.

**4. Can I demonstrate it on one short section of Screen 05 first?** Yes, but it costs World Labs credits. Before spending anything I would give you the exact job and credit cost and wait for your OK. I won't touch other screens unless it works on that section.

**5. What can't I deliver?** "Exactly my approved screen in every frame of genuine 3D gameplay" is beyond what I can build. A 3D environment artist would come closer than I can, but even then it would match your art in style, not pixel for pixel. Anything better than "clearly your screen, with visible differences" would be a guess, not a promise.

Everything you have is saved and unchanged:
- the painted version, `?paint=1`
- both Benny-swimming tests
- the rejected 3D version

Do you want me to quote the credit cost for the one-section Screen 05 test? If not, I'll stop here.

Base directory for this skill: /root/.claude/plugins/cache/worldlabs/worldlabs/0.2.2/skills/atlas-splats

# Atlas splats

`posedImages2Splats` reconstructs a scene from posed views with depth, then refines it into an
SPZ file. It is the final step, and one run takes 15 to 25 minutes.
While refining it generates its own dense views, which it does not return.

What you control is the set of views you give it, so a good result comes from getting that set
right. The views are also the preview of the result.

This file and [references/scene.md](references/scene.md) are the method, and the request shapes
are in `assets/example/`. Read both files in full before starting. The Atlas docs are reference
for a task's fields and limits: open a task's page when a request needs a field these files do
not show, or when one is rejected. The docs also have shorter workflow pages written for people;
where they differ from these files, follow these files.

## Steps

1. **Agree where to work, then build the scene.** Before anything else, check whether Blender
   is installed and ask the person where to work. With Blender installed, the choice is:

   - **Open Blender**, so they can watch the scene build and scrub through it; or
   - **Build in the background** and hand over the `.blend` at the end.

   If they choose the open window, open it as soon as the first image is posed, before any
   views or path, so they watch from the start. Without Blender, work in the shell.
   [references/scene.md](references/scene.md) has the question for each setup and the steps:
   pose the images, build the scene out in rounds of a few views until it is blocked out with no
   gaps, and show it.

2. **Check the set as reconstruction input.** The posed frames and the views you kept are the
   input. A good set:

   - shows every area the person will look at: the floor, low furniture, walls, and the far side
     of anything they will move around. Areas no view shows come out blurry or invented;
   - agrees with itself. An object with a different shape or place in two views becomes a
     doubled, ghosted object;
   - has depth over most of every frame, and one size for all frames. A view can look right and
     still have depth on only a small part of it.

   For a single room, 12 to 16 views in all is a good range. To add coverage, send another
   `atlasGenerate` request with the current views as `contextFrames` and `"returnDepth": true`.

3. **Reconstruct once.** Submit it as soon as the set is good, and tell the person it is
   running and how long it takes. The request lists each frame's image, depth and camera; see
   [the example request](assets/example/splats-request.json).

   ```sh
   worldlabs tasks run posedImages2Splats --request splats.json --json > splats_op.json
   worldlabs operations wait <operation-id> --timeout 3600 --json
   ```

   Submit without `--wait` and keep the operation ID. If the wait times out, wait again. A
   second submission while the first runs starts a second full run.

4. **Hand it over.**

   ```sh
   worldlabs operations download <operation-id> --out splats
   ```

   The result is an SPZ file named for its splat count (`refinedSplats_2000000.spz`), in the
   same world as the cameras you sent. Look at it before you report: from the start view, and
   from places the person will go.

   Give the person the file, a way to look at it, the operation ID, and which parts of the scene
   the model invented. In Blender the splats import into the scene they have been watching.
   Otherwise see [Rendering with Spark](https://docs.atlas.worldlabs.ai/rendering-with-spark.md).

## Example

[A complete run](references/example.md): one photo of a potter's studio, the room built out in
three rounds of views, and one reconstruction from the ten frames, with pictures of the result.
Its requests and results are in `assets/example/`. It shows one scene's choices, not values to
copy.

## Facts

- Bounded, textured interiors reconstruct best. Sky, foliage, thin structures, glass, faces and
  large plain walls are where artifacts appear, and so are surfaces that only one view sees at
  close range. Say so when the scene has them.
- `prompt` describes the scene. Leave it out and Atlas writes one from the images.
- For a mesh, pass the SPZ asset to `splats2Mesh` as `splatAsset`.
- A video of the same scene uses the same views; see the `atlas-flythrough` skill.
- An HTTP 422 means the request was rejected. The CLI does not print the reason; check that
  every frame has `imageAsset`, `depth.depthAsset` and `camera`, and that all cameras share one
  size.
- CLI setup, errors and other tasks are in the `worldlabs-cli` skill. Guides:
  https://docs.atlas.worldlabs.ai/posed-images-to-splats.md and
  https://docs.atlas.worldlabs.ai/splat-best-practices.md

content.content:
with the same request and `--idempotency-key <key>` so the task is not started twice.
- **Result.** A finished operation has `response` or `error`; check `error` first.
  `operations download` saves every output file to a new directory, named for its place in the
  response (`frames_003_image.jpg`, `frames_003_depth.exr`), and writes `operation.json` with
  each file's local path. If the command is missing, update the CLI.
- **Errors.** The CLI does not print the API's reason. HTTP 422 means the request body was
  rejected: check it against the task's guide page. HTTP 402 means the project is out of credits
  or over its spend limit. HTTP 401 or 403 is the key or its permissions. An operation that ends
  `THROTTLED` hit a capacity limit, not a problem with the request: tell the person, wait a few
  minutes, and run it again. See https://docs.atlas.worldlabs.ai/errors.md

Tasks spend the project's credits. Run the tasks the request needs without quoting prices or
asking for a go-ahead; https://docs.atlas.worldlabs.ai/billing.md has the rates if the person
asks. Do not rerun a finished task to see whether the result changes.

## Without a shell

If World Labs tools are connected (`list_projects` and a tool per task, such as
`images2PosedRGBD`), they run the same tasks. A task's tool takes `project_id`,
`idempotency_key`, and `request`, the same request body the task's guide page gives.

----
# Build the scene

A video and splats start the same way: agree how to work, pose the images, and build the scene
out a few views at a time until it is blocked out with no gaps. This file is identical in
`atlas-flythrough` and `atlas-splats`.

Building the scene is also a job on its own. When the person asks for new angles of an image,
the other side of something, or more of a place, do it this way, starting with where to work,
whether or not they have chosen a video or splats yet. Views that already exist from earlier in
the session are the start of the scene: bring them in and keep building from there.

Camera and depth conventions are in [conventions.md](conventions.md). A complete run is in
[example.md](example.md).

## Agree how to work

The person directs and you do the work. Two decisions are theirs:

- **Where the work happens.** Blender is the preferred place when it is installed. Both of you
  see the scene in 3D, they can shape the result, and they keep a project file at the end.
- **What the result should be.** The subject, how far the camera goes, what they want to be able
  to look at.

Asking is the default for those two. Ask each in one short line when it comes up. A plain
request, such as "make me a flythrough", is not a request to skip the questions.

Once they are settled, carry the work through to the finished result without stopping. Show
each stage as it lands (the posed image, each round of views, the path) so the person can steer
whenever they want to. They have asked for the result, so the steps that produce it need no
go-ahead and no price quoted.

Decide for the person only when they say outright that they do not want to be asked, for example
"don't check in, just deliver it". Then choose what they would most likely choose, and say what
you chose. For where to work, that is Blender in the background whenever it is installed.

Where to work comes first, before posing or reading further. Check what is there, then ask the
question that fits:

| What you find | What to ask |
| --- | --- |
| Blender 5.3 or newer, connected (it is open and you can run Python in it through Blender tools), with the Atlas add-on | Work in the open window where they can watch, or in the background and hand over the project at the end? |
| Blender installed, but the Blender tools or the Atlas add-on missing | Set that up now, or work in the background with what is there? Background work needs neither. |
| No Blender | Nothing. Work in the shell, and mention once that Blender would let both of you see the scene in 3D. |

Put the question in the person's terms: what each choice lets them see, and what it needs from
them. Words like "connected" describe your side of it and mean little to them. For example:
"Blender is installed. I can build this in an open Blender window so you can watch it take
shape, which needs Blender open and takes me a minute to link up, or build it in the background
and give you the Blender file at the end. Which would you like?"

`blender --version`, or `/Applications/Blender.app` on a Mac, tells you whether it is installed.
The `atlas-blender` skill covers working in Blender, with or without the add-on. Atlas tasks
themselves always run through the `worldlabs` CLI below, or through the add-on.

With only connected World Labs tools and no shell, the task tools take the same requests. The
depth files usually cannot be read there, so cameras are placed without measuring: stay near
space the image clearly shows as open, generate a few views at a time, and look at each result.

## 1. Pose the images

Upload each image, estimate its camera and depth, and save the result:

```sh
worldlabs assets upload room.jpg --json                    # note the "id"
echo '{"frames":[{"imageAsset":{"assetId":"<id>"}}],"targetResolution":[1280,720]}' > pose.json
worldlabs tasks run images2PosedRGBD --request pose.json --wait --json > pose_op.json
worldlabs operations download <pose-operation-id> --out scene
```

- `targetResolution` sets the grid every later step uses. Choose the size closest to the image's
  shape: `[1280, 720]`, `[960, 720]`, `[528, 704]` or `[720, 1280]`.
- Photos of one real place go in one request, so their cameras share a world.
- Posing puts the scene in a level, Y-up world. Pose an image from `atlasTextToImage` as well: the
  depth that task can return is not levelled.
- `scene/operation.json` holds each frame's camera, and for its image, depth and confidence the
  local `path` and the `assetId`. Later requests name frames by those asset IDs; nothing is
  uploaded again.

## 2. See the scene

Look at the scene before placing anything, and look at it as a picture, not only as numbers. In
Blender the posed frames are cameras with point clouds. In a shell, draw the depth points from
above with the camera on them; walls, furniture and open floor show at a glance.

Find how far away things are, where the floor is, and where there is room to stand. Distances
are in the depth's units, which is what tells you how big a move is. Settle with the person what
the main part of the scene is.

## 3. Build the scene out

One image is a single view of a place. This step decides what the rest of the place is: the far
side of the table, the wall behind the camera, what is round the corner. The model invents
whatever a camera sees that no frame has shown, and here that is the point. A round takes under
a minute, and you and the person see the result before anything is built on it.

Explore the way a person would walk into a room they had only seen in a photo: go in, cross to
the other side, turn round and look back. At this stage the question is what is in this place,
not where a camera path or a viewer will go. That comes after, and it will be better for having
a real scene to choose from.

Work in rounds:

1. **Place a few cameras** that stand somewhere no frame has stood and look at something no
   frame has shown: from one side of the main subject across to the other, from the far end
   back toward where the first camera stood, into a corner, through an opening.
2. **Generate them** as one `atlasGenerate` request, with the frames so far as `contextFrames`
   and `"returnDepth": true`, so each new view joins the scene with its own depth.
3. **Look at what came back.** Each view shows new surfaces and new open space. Drop a view that
   disagrees with the others.
4. **Place the next few** from what the new views revealed: floor that turned out to be open, a

later rounds pass the frames nearest the new cameras as context, not every frame. The

quick.

content.content:
# Billing

Understand credits, projects, spend limits, and payments.

Atlas Developer API usage is billed to the account that owns the API key's
project. Balances, top-ups, and monthly spend limits are under
[Settings → Developer Platform](https://atlas.worldlabs.ai/settings/credits/developer). Payment methods and
invoices are under [Settings → Billing](https://atlas.worldlabs.ai/settings/billing). Account usage is on the
[Settings → Usage](https://atlas.worldlabs.ai/settings/usage/developer) page.

## Credits and top-ups

Developer API tasks draw credits from the account balance. The current
conversion is 1,000 credits per US dollar. Credits purchased for the account
do not expire.

Account owners and billing owners can add credits manually or enable automatic
recharge. Auto-recharge charges the account's default payment method when the
balance falls below a configured threshold and restores it to the chosen
balance.

The task rate card can change. Use the current rate card shown in
the platform when estimating task costs rather than embedding model prices in
client code.

## Frameboy sessions

A Frameboy session in Atlas Studio runs for up to a minute and costs 500
credits ($0.50), charged once, after it ends. It draws on the same credits as
other Studio work. A session is free if it plays for less than 5 seconds, or if
it ends because its server stopped responding.

An account without enough credits cannot start a session: the request returns
`402 Payment Required` with `code` set to `CREDITS_UNAVAILABLE`, and no session
is started or queued. A charge can take a few minutes to appear on the Usage
page.

## Studio tools

Prompt enhancement costs 20 credits ($0.02) a request. An image edit costs 125
credits ($0.125) a request. An image upscale costs 10 credits ($0.01) an image.
A Chisel caption costs 20 credits ($0.02) a request. A Relight image edit costs
what the model provider charged for it, converted to credits.

## Projects and attribution

Create projects to separate credentials, assets, operations, and usage for
different environments or products. Every API key is bound to one project, so
usage is attributed without sending a project ID in each Developer API route.

Project isolation is useful even when one account funds all work:

- production and development can use different keys;
- teams can inspect their own usage;
- experiments can receive a tighter budget;
- a compromised key cannot access another project's resources.

## Usage

The Usage page shows the credits the account spent over a date range, per day
and grouped by task or project. Developer API usage can also be grouped by API
key. Studio and Developer usage are shown separately. Select a day to see its
breakdown. Usage reflects billed charges; a finished task can take a few
minutes to appear.

## Set monthly spend limits

Account owners and billing owners can create a monthly USD spend limit for the
entire account or for one project. Limits reset each calendar month.

When an enabled applicable limit reaches 100%, new Developer API tasks pause.
Tasks already running are allowed to finish. Raising, disabling, or deleting
the limit allows new tasks once the account also has sufficient credits.

Use an account-wide limit for the total safety ceiling, then add project limits
for workloads that need independent guardrails. A project task must satisfy
both limits when both apply.

> Spend limits are guardrails, not exact real-time accounting boundaries.
> In-flight work and delayed usage observations can produce some variance.

## Payment methods and invoices

The account uses one shared Stripe payment profile for API credit purchases,
automatic recharge, and Atlas Studio subscriptions. Account owners and
billing owners can add a payment method, choose the default, open the Stripe
customer portal, and review invoices from the billing page.

Do not put payment operations in an API integration. Billing administration
uses the authenticated platform session and account permissions, not a World
Labs API key.

## When work is paused

If a task is rejected because the account is out of credits or a spend limit is
reached, the response is `402 Payment Required` with `code` set to
`CREDITS_UNAVAILABLE` or `SPEND_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`:

1. Do not retry in a tight loop.
2. Check the API key's project limit and the account-wide limit.
3. Add credits or adjust the appropriate limit.
4. Retry the same logical submission with its original idempotency key.

method.description:
Action to specify what pull request data needs to be retrieved from GitHub. 
Possible options: 
 1. get - Get details of a specific pull request.
 2. get_diff - Get the diff of a pull request.
 3. get_status - Get combined commit status of a head commit in a pull request.
 4. get_files - Get the list of files changed in a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 5. get_commits - Get the list of commits on a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 6. get_review_comments - Get review threads on a pull request. Each thread contains logically grouped review comments made on the same code location during pull request reviews. Returns thread metadata and comments with nullable current and original line-range coordinates (line, start_line, original_line, original_start_line). Current coordinates are omitted when unavailable, such as for outdated comments. Use cursor-based pagination (perPage, after) to control results.
 7. get_reviews - Get the reviews on a pull request. When asked for review comments, use get_review_comments method. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 8. get_comments - Get comments on a pull request. Use this if user doesn't specifically want review comments. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 9. get_check_runs - Get check runs for the head commit of a pull request. Check runs are the individual CI/CD jobs and checks that run on the PR.

> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.worldlabs.ai/llms.txt

# Pricing

> Understanding API usage and credits

## Credits

> [!WARNING]
>
> World API billing is separate from Marble web app billing.
>
> * Credits purchased for the Marble app at [marble.worldlabs.ai](https://marble.worldlabs.ai) CANNOT be used with the API
> * API usage requires credits purchased through the World Labs Platform at [platform.worldlabs.ai](https://platform.worldlabs.ai)
>
> If you plan to use the API, make sure you purchase credits on the World Labs Platform, not in the Marble app.

The World Labs API uses a credit-based pricing model.

You may purchase credits at a fixed rate of \$1.00 USD per 1,250 credits through the [World Labs Platform](https://platform.worldlabs.ai/billing). The minimum purchase is 6,250 credits or \$5.00 USD.

API credits do not expire.

You can check your current API credit balance with
[`GET /marble/v1/credits`](https://docs.worldlabs.ai/api/reference/credits/get).

### Auto-refill

You may enable auto-refill to avoid service interruptions by automatically purchasing credits when your balance is low.

On the [billing page](https://platform.worldlabs.ai/billing), you may enable and configure auto-refill once you have a payment method on file.

You may configure the threshold at which auto-refill is triggered, as well as the target balance to refill to.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Note that when auto-refill is triggered, your balance will not settle at the target balance. This is because the refill is applied before the cost of the API request is deducted from your balance.
>
> For example, assume your threshold is 10,000 credits and your target balance is 20,000 credits, and you have a balance of 10,000 credits.
>
> 1. You make an API request that costs 1,500 credits. We would observe that your balance would drop to 8,500 credits, which is below your threshold.
> 2. The auto-refill would then be triggered and you would be charged to bring your balance to 20,000 credits.
> 3. Finally, your balance would drop to 18,500 credits to charge for the API request.

## Usage events

Credits are consumed as you use the API.

API requests may map to one or more usage events, and each usage event may have its own cost in credits associated with it. The total cost of an API request is the sum of the costs of all the usage events it maps to. The cost of each usage event is determined largely by the compute resources required to complete the underlying operation.

You may view your usage event history in the [usage page](https://platform.worldlabs.ai/usage).

Note that not all API requests consume credits, such as API key creation, media asset upload and management, and Operation polling.

If your credit balance is too low when a request arrives, the API returns
`402 Payment Required` with a response body that links to the
[billing page](https://platform.worldlabs.ai/billing), where you can add
credits or enable auto-refill.

### Overage

The credit check above compares your balance against a low-balance threshold.
It is not a per-request cost estimate, so it does not guarantee that your
remaining balance covers the request it admits. A request that starts while
your balance is low can cost more credits than you have left and take your
balance below zero.

Credits used beyond your prepaid balance are not refused and not written off.
They become an overage. Unlike prepaid credits, which you pay for up front and
draw down as you go, an overage is settled after the fact: at the end of each
monthly billing period, usage your prepaid credits did not cover is converted
to USD at your account's credit rate — \$1.00 USD per 1,250 credits on standard
pay-as-you-go accounts, the same rate at which credits are sold — and charged
to your payment method on file.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Two things about overage charges surprise people:

> Two things about overage charges surprise people:
>
> * **The charge arrives after the usage.** Usage in one month is invoiced at the
>   start of the next, so a charge can land weeks after your last API request.
> * **Auto-refill does not gate it.** Auto-refill only controls whether we top up
>   your balance automatically. Turning it off does not cap your usage and does
>   not prevent an end-of-period overage charge.
>
> To check what an overage charge covers, compare the billing period shown on the
> invoice against your usage events for that period on the
> [usage page](https://platform.worldlabs.ai/usage).
### World generation pricing
Generating a world using the [World Generation API](https://docs.worldlabs.ai/api/reference/worlds/generate.md) is the most common API request. However, the number of usage events and the cost of generating a world depends on the input type.
The World Generation API requires a panorama image (pano) to convert into a 3D world, so it first generates a pano from your input if a pano is not provided. Image prompts use `is_pano: "auto"` by default; when the API detects a valid equirectangular pano, it skips pano generation. As a result, a World Generation API request often includes two usage events:
1. Pano generation (if needed)
2. World generation (from pano)
For **Marble 1.0 / `marble-1.0`** and **Marble 1.1 / `marble-1.1`**, the **world generation** usage event is billed at **1,500 credits**. Draft world generation (`marble-1.0-draft`) is billed at **150 credits**.
For **Marble 1.1 Plus / `marble-1.1-plus`**, a request always includes **1 world generation** event billed at **1,500 credits**. For larger worlds, our system may automatically determine to include up to 1,500 additional credits for variable world generation.
Depending on your input type, you may also incur a **pano generation** usage event. If you generate from an existing pano and the API treats it as a pano, there is no pano generation step, so there is no additional pano generation cost.
#### Usage event costs
| Usage event | Credits |
| - | -: |
| Pano generation (image, pano) | 0 |
| Pano generation (text) | 80 |
| Pano generation (image, non-pano) | 80 |
| Pano generation (multi-image) | 100 |
| Pano generation (video) | 100 |
| Draft world generation | 150 |
| World generation | 1,500 |
| HQ mesh export | 3,500 |
#### Draft model totals (`marble-1.0-draft`)
| Input type | Pano generation | World generation | Total |
| - | -: | -: | -: |
| Image (pano) | 0 | 150 | 150 |
| Text | 80 | 150 | 230 |
| Image (non-pano) | 80 | 150 | 230 |
| Multi-image | 100 | 150 | 250 |
| Video | 100 | 150 | 250 |
#### Standard model totals (`marble-1.0`, `marble-1.1`)
| Input type | Pano generation | World generation | Total |
| - | -: | -: | -: |
| Image (pano) | 0 | 1,500 | 1,500 |
| Text | 80 | 1,500 | 1,580 |
| Image (non-pano) | 80 | 1,500 | 1,580 |
| Multi-image | 100 | 1,500 | 1,600 |
| Video | 100 | 1,500 | 1,600 |
#### Marble 1.1 Plus totals (`marble-1.1-plus`)
| Input type | Pano generation | Base world generation | Variable world generation | Total |
| - | -: | -: | - | - |
| Image (pano) | 0 | 1,500 | 0-1,500 | 1,500-3,000 |
| Text | 80 | 1,500 | 0-1,500 | 1,580-3,080 |
| Image (non-pano) | 80 | 1,500 | 0-1,500 | 1,580-3,080 |
| Multi-image | 100 | 1,500 | 0-1,500 | 1,600-3,100 |
| Video | 100 | 1,500 | 0-1,500 | 1,600-3,100 |
#### Observed Marble 1.1 Plus costs
The variable world generation charge depends on the size of the world,
so actual costs vary by request. The table below shows observed succeeded
`marble-1.1-plus` World Generation API costs through June 25, 2026.
1,250 credits = \$1.00.
| Input type | Mean | Median | P75 | P90 | P95 | P99 | Max |

## Model mapping
The World API currently supports the following Marble models:
| Marble model | API `model` |
| - | - |
| `Marble 1.1 Plus` | `marble-1.1-plus` |
| `Marble 1.1` | `marble-1.1` |

| `Marble 1.0 Draft` | `marble-1.0-draft` |

>
> The API still supports the legacy `model` value for Marble 1.0 models. Support for these legacy values will be removed in a future release.
>
> | Current `model` value | Legacy `model` value |
> | - | - |
> | `marble-1.0` | `Marble 0.1-plus` |
> | `marble-1.0-draft` | `Marble 0.1-mini` |
> [!WARNING]
>
> The API currently supports a default model of `marble-1.0` if no model is specified in order to maintain compability. This will change in a future release to default to `marble-1.1`.

Generating a world using the [World Generation API](https://docs.worldlabs.ai/api/reference/worlds/generate.md) is the most common API request. However, the number of usage events and the cost of generating a world depends on the input type.
The World Generation API requires a panorama image (pano) to convert into a 3D world, so it first generates a pano from your input if a pano is not provided. Image prompts use `is_pano: "auto"` by default; when the API detects a valid equirectangular pano, it skips pano generation. As a result, a World Generation API request often includes two usage events:
1. Pano generation (if needed)
2. World generation (from pano)
For **Marble 1.0 / `marble-1.0`** and **Marble 1.1 / `marble-1.1`**, the **world generation** usage event is billed at **1,500 credits**. Draft world generation (`marble-1.0-draft`) is billed at **150 credits**.
For **Marble 1.1 Plus / `marble-1.1-plus`**, a request always includes **1 world generation** event billed at **1,500 credits**. For larger worlds, our system may automatically determine to include up to 1,500 additional credits for variable world generation.
Depending on your input type, you may also incur a **pano generation** usage event. If you generate from an existing pano and the API treats it as a pano, there is no pano generation step, so there is no additional pano generation cost.

| - | -: |
| Pano generation (image, pano) | 0 |
| Pano generation (text) | 80 |
| Pano generation (image, non-pano) | 80 |
| Pano generation (multi-image) | 100 |
| Pano generation (video) | 100 |
| Draft world generation | 150 |
| World generation | 1,500 |
| HQ mesh export | 3,500 |
#### Draft model totals (`marble-1.0-draft`)
| Input type | Pano generation | World generation | Total |
| - | -: | -: | -: |
| Image (pano) | 0 | 150 | 150 |
| Text | 80 | 150 | 230 |
| Image (non-pano) | 80 | 150 | 230 |
| Multi-image | 100 | 150 | 250 |
| Video | 100 | 150 | 250 |
#### Standard model totals (`marble-1.0`, `marble-1.1`)
| Input type | Pano generation | World generation | Total |
| - | -: | -: | -: |
| Image (pano) | 0 | 1,500 | 1,500 |

| Image (non-pano) | 80 | 1,500 | 1,580 |

"""Marble World API pilot helper (Rainbow Screen 05). The API key is injected by the session proxy;
this script never reads, prints or stores it. Usage:
  marble_pilot.py credits
  marble_pilot.py upload <image.png>                 -> prints media_asset_id
  marble_pilot.py generate <model> <media_asset_id> <display_name> <prompt_file>  -> prints operation id
  marble_pilot.py poll <operation_id> <out.json> [max_seconds]
  marble_pilot.py world <world_id> <out.json>
  marble_pilot.py export_ply <world_id> <resolution> <out.json>
"""
import json, os, sys, time, urllib.request, urllib.error

API = "https://api.worldlabs.ai/marble/v1"
CAP_SPEND = 6250          # user-approved maximum: US$5
START_BALANCE = 7000.0    # balance at the first authentication test (2026-11-16)


def call(method, path, body=None, timeout=60):
    data = json.dumps(body).encode() if body is not None else None
    req = urllib.request.Request(API + path, data=data, method=method)
    req.add_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as r:
            return r.status, json.loads(r.read() or b"{}")
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        try:
            return e.code, json.loads(e.read() or b"{}")
        except Exception:
            return e.code, {}


def credits():
    s, d = call("GET", "/credits")
    return d.get("remaining_credits") if s == 200 else None


def guard(cost):
    bal = credits()
    spent = START_BALANCE - bal
    if spent + cost > CAP_SPEND:
        sys.exit(f"REFUSED: spent {spent:.0f} + {cost} > cap {CAP_SPEND}")
    print(f"budget ok: balance {bal:.0f}, spent so far {spent:.0f}, this job ~{cost}, cap {CAP_SPEND}")


def main():
    cmd = sys.argv[1]
    if cmd == "credits":
        print(credits())
    elif cmd == "upload":
        path = sys.argv[2]
        ext = os.path.splitext(path)[1].lstrip(".").lower()
        s, d = call("POST", "/media-assets:prepare_upload",
                    {"file_name": os.path.basename(path), "kind": "image", "extension": ext})
        if s != 200:
            sys.exit(f"prepare_upload HTTP {s}: {d}")
        info = d["upload_info"]
        req = urllib.request.Request(info["upload_url"], data=open(path, "rb").read(),
                                     method=info.get("upload_method", "PUT"))
        for k, v in (info.get("required_headers") or {}).items():
            req.add_header(k, v)
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=120) as r:
            print("upload HTTP", r.status)
        print("media_asset_id", d["media_asset"]["media_asset_id"])
    elif cmd == "generate":
        model, asset, name, prompt_file = sys.argv[2:6]
        cost = {"marble-1.0-draft": 230, "marble-1.1": 1580, "marble-1.0": 1580}[model]
        guard(cost)
        body = {"display_name": name, "model": model,
                "world_prompt": {"type": "image", "is_pano": False,
                                 "image_prompt": {"source": "media_asset", "media_asset_id": asset},
                                 "text_prompt": open(prompt_file).read().strip()}}
        s, d = call("POST", "/worlds:generate", body)
        print("generate HTTP", s)
        print(json.dumps({k: d.get(k) for k in ("operation_id", "done", "error", "metadata")}, indent=1))
    elif cmd == "poll":
        op, out = sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
        limit = float(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 540
        t0 = time.time()
        while True:
            s, d = call("GET", f"/operations/{op}")
            prog = (d.get("metadata") or {}).get("progress")
            if d.get("done") or s != 200 or time.time() - t0 > limit:
                break
            print(f"{time.time()-t0:5.0f}s {prog}", flush=True)
            time.sleep(15)
        json.dump(d, open(out, "w"), indent=1)
        print("HTTP", s, "done", d.get("done"), "error", d.get("error"))
    elif cmd == "world":
        s, d = call("GET", f"/worlds/{sys.argv[2]}")
        json.dump(d, open(sys.argv[3], "w"), indent=1)
        print("HTTP", s)
    elif cmd == "export_ply":
        wid, res, out = sys.argv[2:5]
        s, d = call("POST", f"/worlds/{wid}:export",
                    {"asset_type": "splats", "format": "ply", "resolution": res}, timeout=600)
        json.dump(d, open(out, "w"), indent=1)
        print("export HTTP", s, "done", d.get("done"), "error", d.get("error"))
    else:
        sys.exit(__doc__)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Rendering Marble SPZ files in third-party engines
> Apply Marble splat scale metadata when rendering SPZ assets outside Marble.
Marble SPZ files are exported in the generated asset coordinate frame. When you
render them outside Marble, use `assets.splats.semantics_metadata` to convert
Gaussian centers and Gaussian sizes into metric, ground-aligned coordinates.
## Read the scale metadata
Completed world responses include SPZ URLs and scale metadata together:
```json theme={null}
{
  "assets": {
    "splats": {
      "spz_urls": {
        "500k": "<500k_spz_url>",
        "100k": "<100k_spz_url>",
        "full_res": "<full_res_spz_url>"
      },
      "semantics_metadata": {
        "metric_scale_factor": 1.23,
        "ground_plane_offset": 0.42
      }
    }
  }
}
```
The numeric values in this example are representative, not fixed constants. Use
the values returned with the world you are rendering.
`metric_scale_factor` converts raw generated asset units to meters.
`ground_plane_offset` places the metric ground plane at `y = 0`.
## Apply center and size scale
Apply scale to Gaussian centers and Gaussian sizes:
```python theme={null}
def to_metric_gaussian(center, linear_scale, semantics):
    scale = semantics["metric_scale_factor"]
    metric_center = center * scale
    metric_center[..., 1] -= semantics["ground_plane_offset"]
    metric_linear_scale = linear_scale * scale
    return metric_center, metric_linear_scale
```
The ground-plane offset applies only to Gaussian centers. Do not apply
`ground_plane_offset` to Gaussian sizes.
## Handle log-scale fields
Some Gaussian splat formats expose `scale_0`, `scale_1`, and `scale_2` as
log-space values. If your decoder gives you log scales, add the logarithm of the
metric scale instead of multiplying the log values directly:
```python theme={null}
import math
def to_metric_log_scale(log_scale, semantics):
    return log_scale + math.log(semantics["metric_scale_factor"])
```
Equivalently, convert to linear scale first:
```python theme={null}
import numpy as np
linear_scale = np.exp(log_scale)
metric_linear_scale = linear_scale * semantics["metric_scale_factor"]
metric_log_scale = np.log(metric_linear_scale)
```

const q = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const W = +(q.get('w') ?? 540), H = +(q.get('h') ?? 960);
const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: false, preserveDrawingBuffer: true });
renderer.setPixelRatio(1); renderer.setSize(W, H); document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
const scene = new THREE.Scene();
const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(+(q.get('fov') ?? 60), W / H, 0.01, 1000);
const spark = new SparkRenderer({ renderer }); scene.add(spark);

scene.add(splat);

window.setView = async (p) => {
  camera.fov = p.fov ?? camera.fov; camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
  camera.position.set(...p.pos); camera.lookAt(new THREE.Vector3(...p.look));
  camera.updateMatrixWorld();
  for (let i = 0; i < (p.frames ?? 6); i++) { renderer.render(scene, camera); await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 120)); }
  renderer.render(scene, camera);
  return true;
};
window.ready = true;
</script></body></html>

import gzip, struct, numpy as np

def read_spz(path):
    raw = gzip.decompress(open(path, 'rb').read())

    o = 16
    pos = np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8, n * 9, o).reshape(n, 3, 3).astype(np.int32); o += n * 9
    v = pos[..., 0] | (pos[..., 1] << 8) | (pos[..., 2] << 16)
    v = np.where(v & 0x800000, v - (1 << 24), v)
    xyz = v.astype(np.float32) / (1 << frac)

    col = np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8, n * 3, o).reshape(n, 3).astype(np.float32); o += n * 3
    rgb = np.clip(0.5 + 0.282095 * ((col / 255.0 - 0.5) / 0.15), 0, 1)

"""Fit the input-picture camera inside a Marble world: homography between a guess render (known camera) and the picture.
python3 -I align.py <render.png> <picture.png> <render_fov> <lookx,looky,lookz> <out.json> [check.jpg]"""
import sys, json, math, numpy as np, cv2
ren_p, ref_p, rfov, look, out = sys.argv[1:6]
W, H = 540, 960
ref = cv2.resize(cv2.imread(ref_p), (W, H)); ren = cv2.resize(cv2.imread(ren_p), (W, H))
sift = cv2.SIFT_create(5000)
k1, d1 = sift.detectAndCompute(cv2.cvtColor(ren, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY), None)
k2, d2 = sift.detectAndCompute(cv2.cvtColor(ref, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY), None)
good = [a for a, b in cv2.BFMatcher().knnMatch(d1, d2, k=2) if a.distance < 0.75 * b.distance]
p1 = np.float32([k1[a.queryIdx].pt for a in good]); p2 = np.float32([k2[a.trainIdx].pt for a in good])
Hm, mask = cv2.findHomography(p1, p2, cv2.RANSAC, 6.0)
f1 = (H / 2) / math.tan(math.radians(float(rfov) / 2)); K1 = np.array([[f1, 0, W / 2], [0, f1, H / 2], [0, 0, 1]])
best = None
for fov2 in np.arange(40, 120, 0.5):
    f2 = (H / 2) / math.tan(math.radians(fov2 / 2)); K2 = np.array([[f2, 0, W / 2], [0, f2, H / 2], [0, 0, 1]])
    R = np.linalg.inv(K2) @ Hm @ K1; R = R / np.cbrt(np.linalg.det(R)); U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(R); Rn = U @ Vt
    e = np.linalg.norm(R - Rn)
    if best is None or e < best[0]: best = (e, fov2, Rn)
e, fov2, R = best
f = np.array([float(x) for x in look.split(',')]); f /= np.linalg.norm(f)
z = -f; x = np.cross([0, 1, 0], z); x /= np.linalg.norm(x); y = np.cross(z, x); M = np.stack([x, y, z], 1)
ow = lambda v: M @ np.array([v[0], -v[1], -v[2]])
fwd = ow(R[2]); up = -ow(R[1]); fwd /= np.linalg.norm(fwd); up /= np.linalg.norm(up)
res = {'matches': len(good), 'inliers': int(mask.sum()), 'fov': float(fov2), 'fit_err': float(e), 'fwd': fwd.tolist(), 'up': up.tolist()}
json.dump(res, open(out, 'w'), indent=1); print(json.dumps(res))
if len(sys.argv) > 6: cv2.imwrite(sys.argv[6], np.concatenate([ref, cv2.warpPerspective(ren, Hm, (W, H))], 1))
EOF

r=json.load(open(S+'/refcam_full.json')); f=np.array(r['fwd']); u=np.array(r['up']); rt=np.cross(f,u); fov=r['fov']
FW,FH=864,1536; fpx=(FH/2)/np.tan(np.radians(fov/2))
n=np.array([-0.377,0.904,0.202]); n/=np.linalg.norm(n); c=np.array([0.148,-0.353,-1.78]); dpl=c@n
def ray(x,y):
    d=f+((x-FW/2)/fpx)*rt+(-(y-FH/2)/fpx)*u; return d/np.linalg.norm(d)
def hit(x,y):
    d=ray(x,y); t=dpl/(d@n); return d*t
L=json.load(open('assets/textures/paint/paint.json')); P05=L['keys'][0]['coins']; sam=np.array(P05['samples'])
pivot=L['keys'][0]['pivot']
# trail: water contact points; start at the painted Benny's waterline
pts=[]; 
for t,x,y,dia in sam:
    yy=y+dia/2
    if yy>pivot[1]: continue

pts=np.array(pts)
B0=hit(pivot[0],pivot[1])
pts=np.vstack([B0,pts])
seg=np.linalg.norm(np.diff(pts,axis=0),axis=1); s=np.r_[0,np.cumsum(seg)]

H=best[1]; print('Benny height above water (to pom top) %.3f'%H)
# coin size: painted coin diameter at sample t -> world diameter
cs=[]
for t,x,y,dia in sam[::8]:
    p=hit(x,y+dia/2); cs.append(dia/fpx*np.linalg.norm(p))
print('coin world diameter (median) %.3f'%np.median(cs[:20]))

# Screen 05 — real 3D test with Marble (round 32, 2026-11-21, branch `claude/screen-05-3d-geometry-9yu7pu`)

**User (verbatim excerpts):** "I want to use my existing 5,420 World Labs Marble credits. I am NOT agreeing to pay $5 cash or purchase additional
credits … Do not purchase anything, charge my card, or start a paid Atlas job." → then "U can use 1580 for full quality from my credits".

## Credits (existing Marble API credits only — ledger `qa/worldlabs/05/pilot/LEDGER.md`)
* Atlas is a separate World Labs product with its own account and credits: NOT usable with these credits, nothing started or bought there.
* Draft world `marble-1.0-draft` (230) → world `f3226155-5633-4e41-bbd5-f58a3f584c26`.
* Full world `marble-1.1` (1,580, user-approved) → world `8bb4cf11-9615-4879-8f2f-8a1cb6002ff7`.
* Balance 5,420 → **3,610**. Every job far below the balance, so no overage / card charge was possible.

## What was done
* Input: the approved Screen 05 as a clean full frame (`input_05_clean.png` = the `?paint=1` plate: painted Benny, coins and HUD removed).
  (The November test used a cropped strip that still had Benny / coins / HUD in it; that is why its lower half was invented.)
* The picture's camera was found inside the world by matching features (`tools/marble05/align.py`): from that camera the 3D world lines up with
  the approved picture (`proof/ALIGN_approved_vs_world_from_picture_camera.jpg`).
* The painted S-path (the coin trail of the approved picture) was projected onto the world's measured water surface (fitted plane, 7–9° from the
  picture's up) → Benny's 3D path. Benny = the improved 3D Benny (`benny31.glb`, its bake, the game's paddling / pom-pom shader, the game's colour
  chain). Follow camera = at the start EXACTLY the picture's camera, then it keeps that relation to Benny along the path (steering followed by half).
* Test viewer (standalone, three.js 0.180 + Spark 2.4.0 splat renderer; the game itself is NOT changed): `tools/marble05/viewer/`
  (`npm i three@0.180.0 @sparkjsdev/spark@2.4.0` in that folder, link the SPZ / GLB / textures as in `play_shots.cjs`, serve, open `play.html`).

## Results (`proof/`)
* `MARBLE05_gameplay_followcam.mp4` — 2.4 s, 30 fps, normal speed, uninterrupted: Benny paddles and steers along the S-path, the bottom gold
  frame passes behind him, the gold rings and purple machinery surround him, coins 1,420 → 1,520.
* `PROOF_APPROVED_vs_3D_GAMEPLAY.jpg` — approved picture | five frames of that run.
* `INSPECT_3D_sheet.jpg` (+ single PNGs) — cameras the player never uses: from in front of Benny, high side, behind wide, OUTSIDE the tunnel
  (a real 3D tube with rings and the coin line inside).
* `TRAVEL_camera_0_to_5_units.jpg` — camera moved forward 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5 units: good to ~2–3 units, then the river smears.
* `BEYOND_good_stretch.png` — what the world looks like past its end (it breaks up).

## Honest verdict
* **Better than every earlier approach for motion:** the first version where Benny really swims forward with a following camera through a 3D world
  that still looks like the approved Screen 05.
* **Too short on its own:** one Marble world holds up for ~3 units of travel ≈ 2.4 s at normal speed (the world is built around one viewpoint;
  most of its detail is within a few tunnel widths). A whole screen would need several overlapping worlds, each 1,580 credits, made from views
  rendered at the end of the previous one — likely drifting further from the approved art each time.
* Remaining differences: softer than the painting, less glow and fewer bubbles; the water is frozen (splats are static — needs an animated water
  layer); Benny's front / sides are plainer than his back; painted coin sprites show a faint square halo up close.
* Android: 500k splats is inside Spark's published Android budget (1–2 million), but a tunnel seen from inside is the heavy case (screen full of
  overlapping splats). Not measured on a phone. Putting it in the game needs three.js 0.170 → ≥ 0.180 (Spark's requirement).

+  (The November test used a cropped strip that still had Benny / coins / HUD in it; that is why its lower half was invented.)
+* The picture's camera was found inside the world by matching features (`tools/marble05/align.py`): from that camera the 3D world lines up with
+  the approved picture (`proof/ALIGN_approved_vs_world_from_picture_camera.jpg`).
+* The painted S-path (the coin trail of the approved picture) was projected onto the world's measured water surface (fitted plane, 7–9° from the
+  picture's up) → Benny's 3D path. Benny = the improved 3D Benny (`benny31.glb`, its bake, the game's paddling / pom-pom shader, the game's colour
+  chain). Follow camera = at the start EXACTLY the picture's camera, then it keeps that relation to Benny along the path (steering followed by half).
+* Test viewer (standalone, three.js 0.180 + Spark 2.4.0 splat renderer; the game itself is NOT changed): `tools/marble05/viewer/`
+  (`npm i three@0.180.0 @sparkjsdev/spark@2.4.0` in that folder, link the SPZ / GLB / textures as in `play_shots.cjs`, serve, open `play.html`).
+
+## Results (`proof/`)
+* `MARBLE05_gameplay_followcam.mp4` — 2.4 s, 30 fps, normal speed, uninterrupted: Benny paddles and steers along the S-path, the bottom gold
+  frame passes behind him, the gold rings and purple machinery surround him, coins 1,420 → 1,520.
+* `PROOF_APPROVED_vs_3D_GAMEPLAY.jpg` — approved picture | five frames of that run.
+* `INSPECT_3D_sheet.jpg` (+ single PNGs) — cameras the player never uses: from in front of Benny, high side, behind wide, OUTSIDE the tunnel
+  (a real 3D tube with rings and the coin line inside).
+* `TRAVEL_camera_0_to_5_units.jpg` — camera moved forward 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5 units: good to ~2–3 units, then the river smears.
+* `BEYOND_good_stretch.png` — what the world looks like past its end (it breaks up).
+
+## Honest verdict
+* **Better than every earlier approach for motion:** the first version where Benny really swims forward with a following camera through a 3D world
+  that still looks like the approved Screen 05.
+* **Too short on its own:** one Marble world holds up for ~3 units of travel ≈ 2.4 s at normal speed (the world is built around one viewpoint;
+  most of its detail is within a few tunnel widths). A whole screen would need several overlapping worlds, each 1,580 credits, made from views
+  rendered at the end of the previous one — likely drifting further from the approved art each time.
+* Remaining differences: softer than the painting, less glow and fewer bubbles; the water is frozen (splats are static — needs an animated water
+  layer); Benny's front / sides are plainer than his back; painted coin sprites show a faint square halo up close.
+* Android: 500k splats is inside Spark's published Android budget (1–2 million), but a tunnel seen from inside is the heavy case (screen full of
+  overlapping splats). Not measured on a phone. Putting it in the game needs three.js 0.170 → ≥ 0.180 (Spark's requirement).

content.text:
Yes, there's a way to do it, and it costs no credits. Real mobile runner games build long levels from repeating pieces. I'd take the sharpest stretch of the 3D world you already paid for, one section of tunnel between two gold rings. Then I repeat it end to end for the whole of Screen 05, joining the pieces at the gold rings, where a seam hides best. Benny swims through all of it with the follow-camera at normal speed.

**What I can't promise:**
- **Repeats:** the same section repeats, so the paddles and the river pattern come back each ring (about once a second).
- **Seams:** a seam may show at a ring if the river doesn't line up perfectly.
- **Softness:** it stays a little softer than your flat painting. It won't get blurrier further in, though, because we always see the sharp part.

Starting the free test now: finding where the gold rings sit in the 3D world.

def read_spz_full(path):
    """All attributes of an SPZ v2 file (SH degree 0): xyz, log scales, quaternion (w, x, y, z), opacity logit, SH DC."""
    raw = gzip.decompress(open(path, 'rb').read())
    magic, version, n, sh, frac, flags, _ = struct.unpack_from('<IIIBBBB', raw, 0)
    assert magic == 0x5053474e and version == 2 and sh == 0, (hex(magic), version, sh)
    o = 16
    pos = np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8, n * 9, o).reshape(n, 3, 3).astype(np.int32); o += n * 9
    v = pos[..., 0] | (pos[..., 1] << 8) | (pos[..., 2] << 16)
    xyz = np.where(v & 0x800000, v - (1 << 24), v).astype(np.float32) / (1 << frac)
    a = np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8, n, o).astype(np.float32) / 255.0; o += n
    col = np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8, n * 3, o).reshape(n, 3).astype(np.float32); o += n * 3
    sc = np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8, n * 3, o).reshape(n, 3).astype(np.float32) / 16.0 - 10.0; o += n * 3
    rq = np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8, n * 3, o).reshape(n, 3).astype(np.float32) / 127.5 - 1.0; o += n * 3
    w = np.sqrt(np.clip(1.0 - (rq ** 2).sum(1), 0, 1))
    a = np.clip(a, 1e-4, 1 - 1e-4)
    return {'xyz': xyz, 'scale': sc, 'rot': np.c_[w, rq], 'opacity': np.log(a / (1 - a)), 'dc': (col / 255.0 - 0.5) / 0.15}


def write_ply(path, d):
    """Standard 3D Gaussian splat PLY (binary little endian)."""
    n = len(d['xyz'])
    props = ['x', 'y', 'z', 'f_dc_0', 'f_dc_1', 'f_dc_2', 'opacity', 'scale_0', 'scale_1', 'scale_2', 'rot_0', 'rot_1', 'rot_2', 'rot_3']
    hdr = 'ply\nformat binary_little_endian 1.0\nelement vertex %d\n' % n + ''.join('property float %s\n' % p for p in props) + 'end_header\n'
    arr = np.c_[d['xyz'], d['dc'], d['opacity'][:, None], d['scale'], d['rot']].astype('<f4')
    with open(path, 'wb') as f:
        f.write(hdr.encode()); f.write(arr.tobytes())

import sys, json, numpy as np

from spz import read_spz_full
src, scene_json, frame_json, out = sys.argv[1:5]

SC = json.load(open(scene_json)); n_plane = np.array(SC['plane']['n'])
L3 = d['xyz'] * np.array([1, -1, -1], np.float32)                     # three.js frame
u = L3 @ ax; h = L3 @ n_plane - dpl; lat = L3 @ rt
UA, UB = 1.30, 3.33                                                     # cut at the start of ring A / ring B
Lt = UB - UA
DH, DLAT = 0.436 - 0.665, -0.022 - 0.0                                  # ring-centre offset B - A (measured cross-sections)
D = ax * Lt + n_plane * DH + rt * DLAT                                  # one copy further on

def ramp(uu, hh):                                                       # floor eased down toward the bay's end (walls untouched)
    wu = np.clip((uu - UA) / Lt, 0, 1); wh = 1 - np.clip((hh - 0.1) / 0.55, 0, 1); wh = wh * wh * (3 - 2 * wh)
    return DH * wu * wh

# Expand
> Expand: Improving low fidelity regions of your world.
[Expand](https://www.youtube.com/embed/SmUlqMmpvCU)
Use Expand to extend your existing worlds beyond their current boundaries.
This tool lets you seamlessly grow your environments by clicking on unexplored areas and
generating new content that naturally connects to your existing world.
## How to access Expand
For any generated world, hit the  **Continue creating** paintbrush icon within the viewer or within your worlds tab to access the Expand tool.
## Getting started with Expand
1. **Navigate your world**: Move around using standard controls to explore your current boundaries
2. **Look for edges**: Find areas where your world meets unexplored space
3. **Check for warnings**: The system shows "Not within recommended area" when you're near expansion zones
4. **Position yourself**: Move to a good viewpoint of the area you want to expand
5. **Click expand**: Press the **Expand** button in the bottom panel
> [!WARNING]
>
> You cannot expand a world generated with Marble 1.1 Plus.
## How to plan strategic expansions
## Advanced expansion techniques
### Strategic positioning
* **Doorway extensions**: Expand beyond doorways to create connected rooms
* **Corner expansions**: Expand from corners to see large new areas
* **Landscape extensions**: Extend outdoor areas to create larger environments
## Common expansion scenarios
### Indoor extensions
* Expand bedrooms into en-suite bathrooms
* Extend kitchens into dining areas or pantries
* Add hallways connecting separate rooms
* Create balconies or terraces from indoor spaces
### Outdoor growth
* Expand gardens into larger landscaped areas
* Extend courtyards into street views or neighboring buildings
* Add pathways leading to new outdoor zones
* Create transitions from indoor to outdoor spaces
### Architectural additions
* Add wings to buildings or structures
* Extend rooflines or architectural features
* Create connecting bridges or walkways
* Add levels or floors to existing structures
## FAQ
### What does "Not within recommended area" mean?
This warning appears when you're either too close to existing content or beyond the limits for expansion. It helps you identify where new content can be generated.
### How do I know where I can expand?
Look for areas where your world meets unexplored or blurry spaces. These boundary zones are where expansion is possible.
### Will new areas match my existing world's style?
Yes, the expansion system analyzes your existing world's visual style, architecture,
and aesthetic to generate new areas that naturally fit and connect with your current environment.
### Can I expand in multiple directions?
Currently, you can perform one expansion of your world in different directions. You can
export the results to studio for stitching.
### What happens if I don't like an expansion?
Each expansion creates a new version while preserving previous states. You can return
to earlier versions or try expanding in different directions from your original world.
### How do expansions connect to existing areas?
The system automatically creates seamless transitions between your existing world and
new areas, ensuring proper lighting, scale, and architectural continuity at the
connection points.

# Multi-image prompt tips
> Specify more details by combining multiple images.
[Multi-image Prompt Tips](https://www.youtube.com/embed/weTbkz5yioc)
# Creating worlds with multiple images with direction control
In the  2D input mode of omnibox, drag in or upload up to 4 images.
Click on the text overlay on image thumbnails to change its direction, and choose one from "Front", "Back", "Left", "Right".
For this mode, images without overlap allow the marble models to creatively fill in the spaces between views.
When you are done specifying the direction of each image, click on  Create to generate the world.
For image file specifications, see [Prompt guidelines →](https://docs.worldlabs.ai/marble/create/prompt-guides.md)
* Direction control is great for connecting different environments creatively.
# Creating worlds with multiple images with Auto Layout
In the  2D input mode of omnibox, drag in or upload up to 8 images.
Toggle "Auto Layout" switch to on so the world model automatically determines the relative positioning of these images.
In this mode, all uploaded images need to share the same aspect ratio and resolution, and should be images from the same space.
Currently images captured in close proximity of each other but covering different viewing directions, and with some overlap between images, work the best.
Click on  Create to generate the world.
* Auto layout is great for quick reconstruction of existing spaces.
> [!NOTE]
>
> Auto Layout works on standard flat images and reconstructs a single space. It does not accept 360° panoramas, and you can upload only one panorama per world (a panorama can't be combined with other images or a video). To build a larger multi-room space such
## What Auto Layout can reconstruct
Auto Layout rebuilds one coherent space from what your images actually show. Parts of the scene the cameras never see, such as behind closed doors, around solid walls, or up a staircase, are generated plausibly to keep the world explorable, so they won't match
For a full multi-room house or building:
* Capture open-plan areas where rooms share sightlines, and shoot from a few overlapping vantage points so most of the space stays in view. A [360 panorama](https://docs.worldlabs.ai/marble/create/prompt-guides/pano-prompt.md) gives the most accurate single-sp
* To connect genuinely separate, walled-off rooms into one walkable building, generate each room on its own and arrange them with [Studio Compose](https://docs.worldlabs.ai/marble/create/studio-tools/compose.md).
## Troubleshooting multi-image issues
### "Auto Layout not working properly"
* **Verify aspect ratios**: Ensure all images have exactly the same width-to-height ratio
* **Check for overlap**: Include visual elements that appear in multiple images
* **Improve image quality**: Use sharp, well-lit images with clear details
* **Check lighting consistency**: Try to match lighting conditions and color temperatures
* **Use images from same location**: Confirm all images are truly of the same space
Multi-image prompting allows you to build more complex, interesting worlds than single images alone.
The key is thoughtful planning of how your images relate spatially and visually to create cohesive, explorable environments.
This documentation is built and hosted on [Mintlify](https://mintlify.com), a developer documentation platform.

For Gaussian splat sizes, renderer coordinate systems, and log-scale `scale_0`
fields, see [Rendering Marble SPZ files in third-party engines](https://docs.worldlabs.ai/api/rendering-spz.md).
### How does API billing work?
Billing for the World API is separate from billing for the Marble web app.
* Credits purchased for the Marble app cannot be used with the API
* API usage requires credits purchased through the World Labs Platform
If you plan to use the API, make sure you purchase credits on the World Labs Platform, NOT in the Marble app.
A Marble subscription — including a Free plan — says nothing about your API billing. The two are separate accounts even when you sign in with the same email, so being on the Marble Free plan does not mean your API usage is free.
### Why was I charged when I have not used the API recently?
Almost certainly this is an overage charge, and it covers an earlier billing period.
API credits are prepaid: you buy them up front and requests draw down that balance, so normal usage produces no charge at all. But requests are admitted based on a low-balance threshold rather than a per-request cost estimate, so a request that starts while your balance is low can cost more than you
That uncovered usage — your overage — is the only part that gets invoiced, and it settles at the end of the monthly billing period rather than at the time of the request. So the charge can arrive weeks after your last request: a charge dated early August covers overage from July. The credits are
Note that having auto-refill disabled does not prevent this. Auto-refill only controls whether your balance is topped up automatically; it does not cap usage.
To reconcile a charge, compare the billing period on the invoice against your usage events for that period on the [usage page](https://platform.worldlabs.ai/usage). See [Pricing](https://docs.worldlabs.ai/api/pricing.md#overage) for details.
### How do I get a panorama image from my world generation?
Every world generation includes a panorama image in the response, accessible via `assets.imagery.pano_url`. This panorama is automatically generated as part of the world creation process.
The panorama URL will be available in the response at `operation.response.assets.imagery.pano_url` or when you fetch the world via `GET /marble/v1/worlds/{world_id}`.
### What is the difference between `marble-1.0`, `marble-1.1`, and `marble-1.1-plus`?
World Labs currently offers three API model variants for world generation:
* `marble-1.0` provides standard world generation at a fixed cost.
* `marble-1.1` provides newer standard world generation at a fixed cost.
* `marble-1.1-plus` provides the most expansive generation path and may add 0-1,500 variable world generation cost for larger worlds, determined automatically by the system during inference.
For the latest pricing details, see the [API pricing page](https://docs.worldlabs.ai/api/pricing.md).
### Where can I read more about World Labs policies?
Please view our [Terms of Service](https://docs.worldlabs.ai/terms-of-service) and [Privacy Policy](https://docs.worldlabs.ai/privacy-policy) for details.
This documentation is built and hosted on [Mintlify](https://mintlify.com), a developer documentation platform.
equirectangular panoramas, such as banners, crops, or collages.
## Multiple images
Use multi-image input when you have several views of the same scene. Add
`azimuth` values when you know where each image faces.
```bash theme={null}
curl -X POST 'https://api.worldlabs.ai/marble/v1/worlds:generate' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'WLT-Api-Key: [REDACTED]' \
  -d '{
    "display_name": "Living Room From Two Views",
    "model": "marble-1.1",
    "world_prompt": {
      "type": "multi-image",
      "multi_image_prompt": [
        {
          "azimuth": 0,
          "content": {
            "source": "uri",
            "uri": "https://example.com/living-room-front.jpg"
          }
        },
        {
          "azimuth": 180,
          "content": {
            "source": "uri",
            "uri": "https://example.com/living-room-back.jpg"
          }
        }
      ],
      "text_prompt": "A cozy living room with a fireplace and bookshelves"
    }
  }'
```
## Local media
For local files, create a media asset, upload to the signed URL, then reference
the returned `media_asset_id` in `world_prompt`. The same flow works for local
images, local panoramas, and local videos.

entries.description: Get details for one or more Hugging Face repos (model, dataset, or space): card metadata, license, downloads, files, Space hardware/status, dataset configs, splits, columns and preview rows. Auto-detects type unless specified. For datasets, use operations: overview, dataset_structure, dataset_preview. Use dataset_structure first to discover configs, splits, sizes, and schema. Use dataset_preview only when config and split are known, unless the dataset has a single config/split.

config.description: Dataset Viewer config. Required for dataset_preview when the dataset has multiple config/split options. Discover via dataset_structure.

limit.description: Row count for dataset_preview. Defaults to 5 and is clamped to 1-100.

offset.description: Row offset for dataset_preview. Defaults to 0.

operations.description: Details to return. Defaults to ["overview"]. For datasets, prefer ["overview", "dataset_structure"] first; then call ["dataset_preview"] with config and split.

repo_ids.description: Repo IDs for (models|dataset/space) - usually in author/name format (e.g. openai/gpt-oss-120b)

split.description: Dataset Viewer split. Required for dataset_preview when the dataset has multiple config/split options. Discover via dataset_structure.

entries.description: Search and list Hugging Face models, datasets and Spaces (sort by downloads, likes, trending) with a shared query interface. You can target models, datasets, spaces, or aggregate across multiple repo types in one call. Include links to repositories in your response.

author.description: Organization or user namespace to filter by (e.g. 'google', 'meta-llama', 'huggingface').

filters.description: Optional hub filter tags. Applied to each selected repo type (e.g. ["text-generation"], ["language:en"], ["mcp-server"]).

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return per selected repo type

query.description: Search term. Leave blank and specify sort + limit to browse trending or recent repositories.

repo_types.description: Repository types to search. Defaults to ["model", "dataset"]. space uses keyword search via /api/spaces.

sort.description: Sort order (descending): trendingScore, downloads, likes, createdAt, lastModified

When to use: Hugging Face Hub models, datasets, Spaces, collections, papers, daily papers, today's trending models, current paper leaderboard, docs; list and read repository files, model and dataset cards (README, license).

Examples:
  {"operations":[{"cmd":"ls","args":["hf://models/trending","--limit","10"]}]}
  {"operations":[{"cmd":"ls","args":["hf://papers/trending"]}]}
  {"operations":[{"cmd":"ls","args":["hf://papers/daily/latest"]}]}
  {"operations":[{"cmd":"cat","args":["hf://papers/2501.00001/paper.md"]}]}
  {"operations":[{"cmd":"search","args":["hf://models","--tag","base_model:finetune:org/repo"]}]}

Use hf_fs for Hugging Face Hub filesystem operations. Call it with operations, an array of {cmd, args} items; multiple operations may be submitted together.

Usage:
  {"operations":[{"cmd":"ls","args":["hf://models/org/repo"]}]}

Grammar; each string below is one args array item:
  ls     URI [--recursive] [--glob GLOB] [--type TYPE] [--sort SORT] [--limit N]
  cat    URI [--offset N] [--max-bytes N]
  attach URI [--max-bytes N]
  stat   URI
  find   URI [--name GLOB] [--path GLOB] [--type TYPE] [--limit N]
  search URI [QUERY] [--type TYPE] [--sort SORT] [--tag TAG] [--kind mcp] [--limit N]

COMMAND = ls|cat|attach|stat|find|search.
TYPE = file|dir|repo|bucket|collection|paper|link.
SORT = createdAt|downloads|likes|lastModified|likes30d|trendingScore|mainSize|id|trending|upvotes.
URI is a canonical hf:// URI. QUERY and GLOB are each one string.

Use search for resource discovery, not repository-content search; ls for a known directory, find for recursive file discovery by name/path (not file contents), stat for filesystem metadata or an uncertain target type, cat for text contents, and attach for a complete JPEG, PNG, or WebP image. When the request gives an exact text-file URI, use cat directly; do not add ls or stat first. stat does not read the contents of JSON, Markdown, or other text files.

Search scopes: hf://models[/OWNER], hf://datasets[/OWNER], hf://spaces[/OWNER], hf://collections[/OWNER], hf://papers, and hf://docs[/...]. Repository and repository-file scopes are not supported: search a resource root or owner scope to discover resources; use find for file discovery within a repository or cat for a known text file. Paper and documentation search require QUERY. --tag filters models, datasets, and Spaces by Hub tag (repeatable; all must match) and applies only to hf://models|datasets|spaces[/OWNER]; omit QUERY when the tag already identifies the target, because QUERY also filters repository names. Derived models carry base_model:ID and base_model:RELATION:ID tags, where RELATION is finetune, adapter, merge, or quantized. --kind applies only to hf://spaces[/OWNER]; the only valid --kind value is mcp, which selects MCP Spaces. Tag families are documented at hf://README.md.
Use ls hf://models/trending, hf://datasets/trending, hf://spaces/trending, or hf://papers/trending for trending listings.
hf://papers/ID is a paper directory, not paper text. Use cat hf://papers/ID/paper.md for paper text and cat hf://papers/ID/metadata.json for metadata. No preliminary listing is needed for these known paths. Use ls hf://papers/ID to discover other resources.
Omit --limit, --sort, and --type unless the request requires them. Limits and path-specific behavior are documented at hf://README.md. Issue one hf_fs call.

Links: hf://models|datasets|spaces/OWNER/NAME/PATH maps to https://huggingface.co[/datasets|/spaces]/OWNER/NAME/resolve/main/PATH (buckets: https://huggingface.co/buckets/OWNER/NAME/resolve/PATH); URL-encode each path segment. arXiv ids (for example 2502.16161) link papers, models and datasets.

args.description: Command arguments. First item must be an hf:// URI, not a local path or bare filename. One argument per array item. search discovers resources, not repository contents; use root/owner discovery scopes, find for file discovery, or cat for a known text file. --tag requires hf://models|datasets|spaces[/OWNER]; --kind requires hf://spaces[/OWNER] and its only valid value is mcp.
